title: Array Traversal: Sum of an Array
oneLiner: Walk an array once with a pointer (here just an index variable marking your position), accumulating as you go.
keyTakeaway: Arrays are contiguous memory (every element stored side by side in one block), so any index is O(1) to read -- the default array technique is one pointer, one linear pass, accumulating something as you go.
explanation: The most fundamental move in array algorithms: visit each element exactly once with an index, and accumulate something as you go (here, a running sum). Almost every array technique you'll learn later -- two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums -- is a variation on this single pass. Step through the visualization to see the pointer move and the sum build up, then implement it yourself and run it against the test cases.

visualizationSteps.message: Start with an array and a running sum of 0. Array: [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
Look at index 0 (value 4). Add it to the running sum -> 4.
Look at index 1 (value 8). Add it to the running sum -> 12.
Look at index 2 (value 15). Add it to the running sum -> 27.
Look at index 3 (value 16). Add it to the running sum -> 43.
Look at index 4 (value 23). Add it to the running sum -> 66.
Look at index 5 (value 42). Add it to the running sum -> 108.
Pointer has passed every index once. Final sum: 108. This one pass, O(n) walk is the shape almost every array algorithm starts from.

complexity.note: One pass touching each element once; only a running total is stored.
